query: Investigate the synthesis of a Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co multi-principal element alloy via high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering. The starting material is a ball-milled powder exhibiting a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution. The processing challenge is that magnesium volatility limits the maximum sintering temperature to 1000 °C, while insufficient driving force below 800 °C prevents bulk formation. Existing literature indicates that differences in atomic properties often lead to stable intermetallics and that oxygen intake during milling is a persistent risk. The specific gap is the kinetic mechanism by which high-temperature sintering promotes a specific microstructural evolution that simultaneously enhances hardness, density, and barrier formation for oxidation/corrosion resistance. Request a hypothesis detailing the interplay between sintering temperature, diffusion activity, and the precipitation of secondary phases that act as diffusion barriers. Provide the boundary condition where this mechanism fails (e.g., excessive temperature causing composition deviation), and a falsification experiment involving post-mortem analysis of the passive film structure and oxidation kinetics to distinguish between a diffusion-controlled mechanism and a surface-reaction-limited one.

generation.hypothesis: The synthesis of a Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co multi-principal element alloy via high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering will result in a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with precipitated secondary phases that act as diffusion barriers, enhancing hardness, density, and barrier formation for oxidation/corrosion resistance.

generation.intervention: Spark plasma sintering at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C
generation.conditions: High-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering under controlled atmosphere
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitated secondary phases, such as Laves phases or oxides
generation.mechanism: Diffusion-controlled mechanism, where the precipitated phases act as diffusion barriers, enhancing hardness and density
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced hardness, density, and barrier formation for oxidation/corrosion resistance
generation.boundary: Excessive temperature (above 1000 °C) causing composition deviation and degradation of properties
generation.uncertainty: The exact role of magnesium volatility and oxygen intake during milling on the final microstructure and properties

falsification_experiment.design: Post-mortem analysis of the passive film structure and oxidation kinetics
measurements: Microstructure analysis using SEM and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation kinetics are not consistent with a diffusion-controlled mechanism, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
